documentation.range:
The Whale Shark is a circum-tropical species, found in all equatorial to warm temperate oceans and adjacent open seas. The core distribution of the species is between approximately 30°N and 30°S. The seasonal expansion of Whale Sharks’ range into temperate waters is associated with sea surface temperature and correlated with the 21–22 ºC isotherm (Duffy 2002, Afonso et al. 2014, Tomita et al. 2014). Their regular seasonal range is presumed to be gradually expanding as the 21–22 ºC isotherm moves polewards in both hemispheres. In the Atlantic Ocean, this is evidenced by increasing sightings in the Azores Archipelago (Afonso et al. 2014), and the first continental European record from Portugal in 2011 (Rodrigues et al. 2012). Whale Sharks have now also been documented in the Mediterranean Sea, from Spain in 2022 (Fortič et al. 2023) and Türkiye in 2021 (Turan et al. 2021), although it is possible sharks could enter from the Red Sea via the Suez Canal as Lessepsian migrants (AFP 2011).

Important sites for feeding, aggregation, migration, and reproduction have been identified across several regions of the world through the Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRA) project (www.sharkrayareas.org; Jabado et al. 2023a, 2023b, 2024, 2025). Some sites of particular importance include the largest known seasonal aggregation off the Yucatán coast of Mexico, with up to 420 individuals feeding in an 18 km² area (de la Parra Venegas et al. 2011). Over 1,300 individual sharks have been identified from this area (Araujo et al. 2022a, Womersley et al. 2024a). Additional significant aggregation sites in the western Atlantic area include the northern Gulf of Mexico, where over 800 Whale Shark sightings were recorded from 1989–2016, including groups of up to 150 sharks (Hoffmayer et al. 2013, 2021). Large numbers (>400) of Whale Sharks also aggregate to feed in the Al Shaheen area off Qatar on occasion (Robinson et al. 2016, M. Jaidah pers. comm. 2025). Over 2,500 sharks have been photo-identified at Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia (B. Norman unpubl. data 2025). Darwin Island in the Galápagos has been identified as particularly important for large adult female Whale Sharks, a demographic class that is rarely sighted elsewhere (Hearn et al. 2016, Rohner et al. 2021), with over 650 individuals identified (Galapagos Whale Shark Project unpubl. data 2025). St. Helena Island in the central South Atlantic is an important habitat for adult sharks, with over 450 individual Whale Sharks identified (Perry et al. 2020, Womersley et al. 2024a), and reproductive behaviours noted (Perry et al. 2020).
documentation.population:
Global population structure
Two global-scale genetic studies on Whale Sharks have estimated genetic effective population size (the number of breeding adults), albeit based on small sample sizes of 70 (Castro et al. 2007) and 68 sharks (Schmidt et al. 2009). Castro et al. (2007) used mitochondrial DNA to estimate current genetic effective population size to be 119,000–238,000 female sharks. Schmidt et al. (2009) estimated genetic effective population size to be 103,572 female sharks, with a standard error of 27,401–179,794, based on microsatellite analysis. However, the lack of knowledge on species-specific mutation rates mean these estimates should be viewed as rough approximations and they may not reflect recent population declines (Schmidt 2021).

Whale Sharks can be individually identified by their characteristic spots and markings, which has allowed for abundance, residency, and connectivity to be assessed within and among aggregation sites across their distribution (Arzoumanian et al. 2005). Most researchers and community contributors are using Sharkbook.ai (formerly whaleshark.org), a global collaborative photo-identification platform, to collate and share individual sighting data. As of March 2025, 15,740 individual Whale Sharks had been identified globally since 1985 (Sharkbook.ai unpubl. data). Long-term studies at aggregation sites around the world have identified hundreds to low thousands of individuals. For instance, at the largest-known aggregation site in the world, Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia, approx. 2,500 individual sharks have been identified since the 1980s (from >30,000 shark encounters; B. Norman unpubl. data 2025).

A caveat is that coastal feeding areas, in particular, are generally biased towards juvenile male Whale Sharks (Norman et al. 2017, Rohner et al. 2021). This complicates trend modelling, and any attempt to use individual counts as a form of census, as the full demographic structure of the regional population is clearly not being ‘captured’ by sight-resight studies. In the global identification dataset referenced above, for the individual sharks where sex was available, 63% (7,046) of sharks were male and 37% (4,209) were female. This provides some insight into the demographic bias in this global dataset (Sharkbook.ai unpubl. data 2025).

Multiple global genetic studies, using both mitochondrial DNA and microsatellite analysis, have demonstrated that the Whale Shark subpopulations in the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific are functionally separate, with more limited differentiation within the large Indo-Pacific region (Castro et al. 2007, Schmidt et al. 2009, Vignaud et al. 2014, Meekan et al. 2017, Yagishita et al. 2020, Guzmán et al. 2021, Hardenstine et al. 2022). Based on these results, we have considered these areas as two separate subpopulations in this assessment.

Yagishita et al. (2020) estimated the global distribution of (genetic) effective population size to be 63% in the Indo-Pacific vs 37% in the Atlantic. Suitable Whale Shark habitat, estimated from Womersley et al. (2024b) at >50% suitability, is distributed 78% Indo-Pacific, and 22% Atlantic (C. Rohner unpubl. data 2025). The global 1985–2025 individual-based dataset from Sharkbook.ai identified 12,459 sharks (80.5%) from the Indo-Pacific and 3,018 sharks (19.5%) from the Atlantic (Sharkbook.ai unpubl. data 2025). On balance, we infer here that approximately 75% of the global Whale Shark population occurs in the Indo-Pacific, and 25% in the Atlantic.

Atlantic Ocean
The only broad-scale sighting data available from the Atlantic subpopulation originate from tuna fleet observers and logbooks from the eastern Atlantic (Sequeira et al. 2014, Escalle et al. 2016b), which showed no clear temporal trend between 1980–2010. Few other long-term trend data exist from the Atlantic.

An expert survey of Whale Shark researchers working at most of the world’s aggregation sites (Womersley et al. 2024a) noted that the largest-known Atlantic aggregation, in the southern Gulf of Mexico and northern Caribbean Sea, is perceived to be decreasing, with the aggregation rarely exceeding 180 animals (R. Graham pers. obs., Cardenas-Palomo et al. 2024). Cardenas-Palomo et al. (2024) documented an overall decline in Whale Shark density in the area from aerial surveys, from 36 sharks/km² in 2016 to 5 sharks/km² in 2021, with an outlier occurring in 2020 (48 sharks/km²), though this trend was not significant. The largest aggregation observed was 170 individuals; much smaller than the >400 individuals reported in 2009 by de la Parra-Venegas et al. (2011) from this aggregation. Trujillo-Cordova et al. (2020) also documented a slight decline in Whale Shark abundance at the site from 2016–2018, and noted the number of sharks/flight was down from 67.5 sharks/flight (2005–2009; de la Parra-Venegas et al. 2011) to 56.0 sharks/flight (2016–2018), a 17% decline. Whale Shark sightings are also perceived to be declining in the northern Gulf, and no Whale Sharks have been sighted since 2019 during dedicated surveys at the Ewing Bank off the Louisiana coast of the United States of America (US) (E. Hoffmayer pers. comm. 2025).

At Gladden Spit in Belize, Whale Shark sightings declined from a mean of 4–6 sharks per day between 1998 and 2001 to fewer than two per day in 2003 (Graham and Roberts 2007), with reports from diving guides indicating that numbers remained low until at least 2016, to current cessation of the aggregation and rare visitation of Whale Sharks to the site (R. Graham unpubl. data 2025). Whale Shark sightings in the Azores have increased in conjunction with the gradual shift northward of the 22ºC isotherm moving through the archipelago (Afonso et al. 2014, Fontes et al. 2020). This positive trend is therefore assumed to correlate directly with environmental change, rather than representing a broader regional increase in shark abundance. Recent perception is that the population trend is neutral in the area (Womersley et al. 2024a). Sightings may have increased in Venezuela (Sánchez et al. 2020) and are slightly increasing at St Helena (Womersley et al. 2024a).

Indo-Pacific
A large fishery for Whale Sharks was present off the Gujarat coast of India, catching an estimated 600 individuals during a dedicated survey from 1999–2000 (Hanfee 2001). The species was protected in 2001. While no quantitative trend data were provided, due to the difficulty of assessing effort, Pravin et al. (1998) observed that “the number of Whale Sharks landed has dwindled and the size and length of the fish landed has reduced considerably in recent years.”

In the Maldives, catches declined from 30 sharks per annum at one major fishing location in the early 1980s to 20 or fewer across the entire country by 1993 (Anderson and Ahmed 1993). A declining abundance of the resident population in the Maldives was documented from 2014–2019 (Harvey-Carroll et al. 2021), and perception is that sightings are decreasing (Womersley et al. 2024a).

In the Mozambique Channel and broader Western Indian Ocean, sightings increased slightly between 1991–2000 before decreasing from 2000–2007, with an overall significant decrease of approximately 66% from 1991–2007. In absolute terms, 600 sightings were reported from the 1990s, decreasing to ~200 across 2000–2007, with peak monthly sightings decreasing by around 50% (Sequeira et al. 2013). In Inhambane, Mozambique, sightings declined 79% between 2005–2011 (Rohner et al. 2013) and, in an updated analysis, sightings at this aggregation declined 87% and individual abundance declined 89% from 2005–2019 (C. Rohner unpubl. data 2025). Sharks >7 m total length (TL) showed a 99% decline in Mozambique between 2005–2019 (C. Rohner unpubl. data 2025). A decline has also been noted in Kenyan sightings (Oddenyo et al. 2018) and Whale Shark sightings largely ceased off Mahé in the Seychelles by 2015, though a large population was documented before 2009 (Rowat et al. 2011, D. Rowat pers. comm. 2020), leading to an 8-year cessation of Whale Shark tourism before increased sightings from 2022 (C. Mason-Parker pers. comm. 2025). Analyses showed a stable abundance trend at Mafia Island in Tanzania from 2012–2019 (Rohner et al. 2022), and from 2015–2019 off Nosy Be in Madagascar (Diamant et al. 2021), although sightings off Nosy Be have subsequently decreased (Womersley et al. 2024a, S. Diamant pers. comm. 2025).

Expert surveys by Womersley et al. (2024a) found that the sighting trend off Djibouti is perceived as neutral, as are sightings at Shib Habil along the Saudi Arabian coast of the Red Sea, while sightings in the Bay of Aqaba in the Red Sea are perceived to be decreasing. Sighting trends at Al Shaheen (Qatar) and Jana (Saudi Arabia) in the Arabian/Persian Gulf, the Daymaniyat Islands and Musandam in Oman, and off Pakistan, were all perceived as neutral (Womersley et al. 2024a). However, the mean size of sharks present at the large aggregation at Al Shaheen has declined from 6.9 m TL in 2011–2014 to 5.7 m TL in 2022–2024, with the proportion of mature male sharks decreasing from 63% to 31% (Robinson et al. 2016, G. Araujo unpubl. data 2025).

Two hundred and fifty-three Whale Shark sightings were recorded by a local dive charter company in the Andaman Sea, Thailand, between 1991–2001 (Theberge and Dearden 2006). Sightings-per-unit-effort showed a significant decline over this period, with an overall decrease from 1.58 Whale Sharks per trip in 1992–1993 to 0.13 sharks per trip in 2000–2001 (Theberge and Dearden 2006). A low absolute number of sightings persisted until at least the 2002–2003 season, although effort data were not recorded (Theberge and Dearden 2006). Recent perception from western Thailand is that the sighting trend is neutral (Womersley et al. 2024a). Separate work in the Koh Tao area in the Gulf of Thailand from 2004–2019 reported a small mean size of 3.7 m (Magson et al. 2022), and local perception is that sightings are slightly increasing (Womersley et al. 2024a). Perception from Malaysian waters is that Whale Shark sightings are increasing (Womersley et al. 2024a).

Whale Sharks were fished in the Philippines prior to protection in 1998, with Whale Shark catch-per-unit-effort (i.e., per boat) declining from 4.44 to 1.7 in Pamilacan and 10 to 3.8 in Guiwanon between two surveys conducted in 1993 and 1997 (Alava and Dolumbaló 2002). Perceived sighting trends have also been assessed for several sites in the Philippines and Indonesia where Whale Sharks are provisioned, i.e., incentivised with food to visit a location for tourism purposes. This means that trend observations have substantial caveats. In the Philippines, sightings are perceived to be slightly increasing at Oslob, and in Indonesia, sightings are neutral at Cenderawasih Bay, Saleh Bay, Derawan Island and Talisayan, increasing at Kaimana, and slightly decreasing at Gorontalo (Womersley et al. 2024a). At ‘natural’ tourism sites in the Philippines, Whale Sharks are perceived to be slightly increasing at Donsol and Pintuyan, and increasing at Honda Bay (Womersley et al. 2024a).

Bradshaw et al. (2008) analysed tourism sightings at Ningaloo Reef, Australia, between 1995–2004, corrected for search effort and environmental fluctuation, and identified a 40% decline in sighting rate and a decline in mean shark length of 1.6 m TL over this time period (based largely on tourism industry size estimates, which are known to be imprecise; B. Norman pers. obs.). Seasonal shifts in peak abundance to outside observation months in that study may have contributed to this observed decline in sighting rate (Mau and Wilson 2007, Holmberg et al. 2009). Analysis of individual sighting data from 1995–2006 identified behavioural heterogeneity in the sharks at Ningaloo, with the majority showing some site fidelity in that they were sighted in multiple seasons (Holmberg et al. 2008). This (majority) subset of the study population was increasing over the course of this work (Holmberg et al. 2008). Follow-up analyses on a slightly longer dataset (1995–2008) confirmed this result, with smaller individuals contributing in larger numbers to recruitment, thereby potentially explaining the observed decline in mean size (Holmberg et al. 2009). However, a genetic study on Ningaloo sharks indicated declining genetic diversity over five consecutive years for mtDNA (2007–2012) and two (2010–2012) for microsatellites (Vignaud et al. 2014). An updated analysis on Whale Shark size at Ningaloo Reef noted that the largest individuals (>10 m TL) were only sighted prior to 2003 (Sequeira et al. 2016). Recent expert perception of this aggregation is that the population trend is neutral (Womersley et al. 2024a).

A commercial fishery for Whale Sharks existed in Taiwan until 2007 (Hsu et al. 2012). Information provided by fishers operating from Hongchun harbour in southern Taiwan indicated that 50–60 sharks were caught each season in the mid-1980s, declining to less than 10 per year in 1994 and 1995 (Chen and Phipps 2002). Although definitive catch trends are not available, there was a significant (58%) decrease in the estimated annual catch in 1997 of 272 sharks (Chen and Phipps 2002) to a reported catch of 113 sharks over 15 months in 2001–2002 (Chen and Phipps 2002). A decline in the mean total length of landed sharks was noted between 2002–2007 (Hsu et al. 2012). A decrease in the mean size of landed sharks was also noted in southern Chinese waters, from 8.27 m TL prior to 2004 to 6.3 m TL in 2008–2011 (Li et al. 2012). Recent perception is that sightings are increasing from Taiwan (Womersley et al. 2024a). However, large Whale Sharks (>10 m TL), as were reported from fisheries in the 1990s (Chen et al. 1997), are rare (H Hsu. pers. comm. 2025).

A decline in Whale Shark interactions with tuna fisheries occurred across much of the Pacific Ocean between 2006–2016, declining from approximately 13–17 interactions per 1,000 sets between 2006 and 2008 to a relatively stable mean interaction rate of approximately eight interactions per 1,000 sets between 2009 and 2016 (Neubauer et al. 2018). Interactions between Whale Sharks and Eastern Pacific tuna fisheries similarly showed a general decline from 2003–2016 (Román et al. 2018). A smaller dataset of tuna fisheries interactions in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean found a weak linear increase in Whale Shark sightings, from around 10 in total per year in the early 2000s to 35 in 2010 (Sequeira et al. 2014).

Interviews with long-term dive guides and researcher perceptions indicate stable sightings of Whale Sharks around Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands (Peñaherrera-Palma et al. 2018, Womersley et al. 2024a). At Cocos Island, Costa Rica, data showed a 6% annual increase in Whale Shark relative abundance per year from 1993–2019, though sharks were only recorded on 2.1% of dives overall (Saltzman and White 2023). This increase was primarily correlated to sea temperature at depth and underwater visibility, suggesting a relationship with El Niño-Southern Oscillation climate variation (Saltzman and White 2023). Sighting trends at La Paz in Mexico and Hawaii are perceived to be neutral (Womersley et al. 2024a). Whale Shark sightings along the coast of Peru have significantly declined despite an increase in monitoring efforts since 2022 (A. Mendoza pers. comm. 2025).

A general observation is that, where rapid declines have been documented, these often occurred during the 1990s and 2000s. A decline in sightings of mature Whale Sharks is also notable in many locations with longer-term (>10-year) datasets. A caution with the data reported above is the limited research and tourism history at many locations, where only expert perception information on trend is available. A ‘shifting baseline’ effect on abundance and size-frequency data may exist.

Global population trend
Overall, in the Atlantic, a population reduction of more than 30% over the last three generations (120 years) is inferred. In the Indo-Pacific, a population reduction of more than 65% over the last three generations is inferred. Combining data from both regions, based on abundance data and actual levels of exploitation, there has been an inferred reduction in the global population size of at least 60% over the last three generations (120 years).
documentation.habitats:
Whale Sharks are found in both coastal and oceanic habitats (Rowat and Brooks 2012, Hearn et al. 2021). This species is highly mobile, with mean daily movement rates ranging from 13.5 km (off Qatar; Reynolds et al. 2022) to >40 km per day (off the Galápagos Islands; Hearn et al. 2021). Sightings have often been correlated with sea surface temperature (SST), often with peak sightings in SSTs between 23–30ºC (Sequeira et al. 2012, Escalle et al. 2016b, Reynolds et al. 2022), and in areas of high primary productivity (Escalle et al. 2016b, Ryan et al. 2017, Rohner et al. 2018).

Whale Sharks spend the majority of time in the epipelagic zone, but dive to at least 1,928 m in depth (Tyminski et al. 2015). The driver of these deep dives is unclear, and may vary according to context. Rhythmic dives may be related to foraging behaviour (Graham et al. 2005), especially when crossing oceanic waters with comparatively low surface productivity (Sleeman et al. 2010, Brunnschweiler and Sims 2011, Tyminski et al. 2015). Deep dives may also be associated with navigation (Tyminski et al. 2015) and/or assist with energy conservation when moving between prey zones (Gleiss et al. 2011).

The largest recorded Whale Shark was approximately 20 m in total length (TL) and 34 tonnes (t) in mass (Chen et al. 1997), with a different individual recorded at 42 t (Hsu et al. 2014), both from Taiwan. An individual extrapolated to be 18.8 m TL was caught in India (Borrell et al. 2011). However, Whale Shark growth is likely determinate, with an asymptotic size of 8.5–8.9 m TL in males and 14.55 m TL in female sharks estimated from Western Australia field data (Meekan et al. 2020), which is supported by length-frequency field data on population structure from elsewhere (Rohner et al. 2015, Pierce et al. 2021b). The maximum observed age of a Whale Shark, based on a vertebral centrum count, is 50 years based on a 10 m TL female shark, the largest Whale Shark aged to date (a 9.9 m TL male in the same study was aged at 35 years) (Ong et al. 2020). Females mature at ~9–10 m TL, with no known regional variation (Joung et al. 1996, Beckley et al. 1997, Hsu et al. 2014, Pierce et al. 2021b). In contrast, the size at which 50% of male Whale Sharks are mature varies from 6.8 m TL at Donsol in the Philippines (McCoy et al. 2018) to 9.2 m TL in eastern Africa (Rohner et al. 2015). Age-at-maturity is estimated at around 25 years for male sharks (Pierce et al. 2021b), with females likely growing more slowly and attaining maturity at a later age (Meekan et al. 2020). Acknowledging the lack of data for female sharks, Pierce et al. (2021b) created a demographic model for the species with two scenarios, either an ‘age of first reproduction’ (following maturity by ~2 years, see below) of 30, or a more conservative estimate of 40 years. Based on these studies, and assuming a 30 year age at female maturity and 50 year maximum observed age, generation length for the Whale Shark is estimated at 40 years.

Reproduction is lecithotrophic (yolk-sac viviparous) with a likely biennial or longer reproductive interval (Pierce et al. 2021b, Rowat et al. 2021a). The single pregnant female documented and examined, from Taiwan, had around 300 pups in various stages of development (Joung et al. 1996). The largest size class of embryos, 58–64 cm TL, appeared close to fully developed (Joung et al. 1996). The smallest free-swimming neonate found in the wild, from the Philippines, was 46 cm TL (Aca and Schmidt 2011). Size-at-birth is therefore presumed to be around this range (Aca and Schmidt 2011). Few neonate Whale Sharks have been reported; a global search by Womersley et al. (2025) collated only 25 individuals less than ≤100 cm TL. It is plausible that, as with adult females, neonatal habitat is in the open ocean (Rohner et al. 2021, Womersley et al. 2025). Most coastal sightings of Whale Sharks occur at feeding areas where the sharks aggregate at the surface to exploit seasonal productivity such as fish spawning events or zooplankton blooms (Rowat and Brooks 2012). A degree of inter-annual site fidelity has been documented in many locations (Araujo et al. 2022a). Sexual- and size-based segregation is typical in these locations, with a bias towards juvenile males from 4–8 m TL (Graham and Roberts 2007, Norman et al. 2017, Rohner et al. 2021). This pronounced segregation indicates that ontogenetic and sex-specific habitat use is prevalent in the species, with adult female sharks in particular rarely sighted (or tracked) in <200 m depth coastal waters (Rohner et al. 2021).
documentation.threats:
The major known contemporary threats to Whale Sharks, on a global scale, are mortality from accidental catch in fisheries as well as suspected mortality from vessel strikes (Pierce et al. 2021a, Rowat et al. 2021b, Womersley et al. 2022, 2024a). Other threats affect Whale Sharks at local or regional scales, including unmanaged wildlife tourism and pollution (Rowat et al. 2021b, Womersley et al. 2024a). Climate change is already thought to be affecting the seasonal extent of Whale Shark distribution, and some areas within their contemporary range may become less suitable habitat for the species and their prey in the future (Reynolds et al. 2024, Womersley et al. 2024b). 

Fisheries
Commercial fisheries for Whale Sharks are presumed to be the primary source of anthropogenic mortality that has caused global population decline. While targeted fisheries, such as those previously present in India, Pakistan, the Maldives, the Philippines, and Taiwan, have largely closed as a result of conservation and management efforts, present-day catches in China remain unclear. Even though the species is protected, small quantities of Whale Shark products have been reported from Chinese trade surveys between 2009–2016 (O'Malley et al. 2017, Steinke et al. 2017) following large catches being documented through interview-based surveys at fishing harbours and processing centres from 2008–2010 (Li et al. 2012). 

Whale Sharks are commonly incidentally captured in tuna purse-seine fisheries (Clarke 2015, Escalle et al. 2016a, Román et al. 2018). Whale Sharks, which are often associated with tuna in oceanic waters, are encircled in large nets along with the tuna species that are the intended catch. While Whale Sharks are usually released, a few are accidentally killed (Clarke 2015, Román et al. 2018). For example, data from observers aboard purse-seine tuna vessels in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean have documented a high density of Whale Shark sightings north of Papua New Guinea, with 1,809 interactions with the fleet (i.e., Whale Sharks encircled in nets) noted between 2006–2016 (Neubauer et al. 2018). However, more recent applications of safe release practices appear to minimize at least short-term mortality (Capietto et al. 2014; Escalle et al. 2016a, 2018). An expert survey estimated a 10% post-release mortality rate in the Western Central Pacific Ocean, although uncertainty was large (Neubauer et al. 2018). Where poor release practices are used, though, such as lifting the sharks from the water by their tails or leaving ropes attached to the sharks following release, longer-term mortality is still likely to be an issue. 

Whale Sharks are also caught in pelagic gillnet (driftnet) fisheries. Limited information is available on Whale Shark catches in tuna gillnet fisheries, which are primarily located in the northern Indian and Pacific oceans. This is a major international fishery, accounting for approximately 34% of Indian Ocean tuna catches (Anderson et al. 2020), and the Indonesian fleet (which operates mostly in the western Pacific) was estimated to exceed 280,000 vessels in 2011 (Anderson et al. 2020). The gillnets, which are designed for entangling tuna and other pelagic fish, can be over 30 km in length (Anderson et al. 2020). Observers have been placed on a few Pakistan-based vessels or recruited from within working crews to monitor incidental catch (Razzaque et al. 2020). Whale Sharks are certainly caught in this fishery, and although live release is possible (Razzaque et al. 2020), few other data are available. A concerning incidental catch of cetaceans (whales and dolphins) from the Indian Ocean tuna gillnet fishery, estimated at 4.1 million individuals from 1950–2018 (Anderson et al. 2020), indicates that this fishery should also be treated as a major threat to Whale Sharks. Large pelagic and coastal gillnet fisheries off Peru (Rojas-Perea et al. 2024) are also known to entangle Whale Sharks (Pajuelo et al. 2018, Guidino et al. 2024).

Whale Sharks are often caught accidentally in large nets set for other species across much of their distribution, with frequent reports coming from coastal gillnet fisheries (i.e., Akhilesh et al. 2013, Barbosa-Filho et al. 2016, Rohner et al. 2018, 2020). While some are released alive, with survival confirmed through post-release monitoring (R. Matsumoto pers. comm. 2025), others are dead when found or killed for their meat or fins (Akhilesh et al. 2013, Pajuelo et al. 2018, Rohner et al. 2018, Wyatt et al. 2019, Sánchez et al. 2020). Most catches are likely to go unreported unless specific surveys are conducted (e.g., Temple et al. 2019; Haque et al. 2021). In Taiwan and elsewhere, concerns remain on current release practices from net fisheries; a rope on the caudal fin is usually used to drag or lift the Whale Sharks out of the set nets, if the rope is cut to release the shark, it may still be attached to the peduncle, causing likely injury or mortality (H. Hsu pers. comm. 2025), and lifting the sharks fully out of the water by the peduncle may cause internal injuries and separation of the caudal fin from the body of the animal reducing likelihood of survival (R. Graham unpubl. data 2025). Furthermore, reports of Whale Shark strandings from Indonesia (Fahmi pers. comm. 06/06/2025) and across the northwestern Indian Ocean (D. Robinson et al. unpubl. data 2025) suggest that mortality from incidental catches can be high and remains unquantified.

Whale Sharks are incidentally caught and their fins opportunistically harvested, for example, in Pakistan (Moazzam Khan pers. comm. 03/06/2025), and the Myeik Archipelago, southern Myanmar, where 3–5 individual Whale Sharks are caught annually (T. Gyi pers. comm. 2025). In southern Java, Indonesia, 10–30 Whale Sharks were landed annually as of 2022 – most caught incidentally and landed locally, with meat, liver and fins entering the local trade (Nijman 2023). In northern Mindanao and Southern Leyte, Philippines, Whale Sharks are occasionally caught in small-scale fisheries (multi-small vessel operated nets) but are released (not always alive; G. Araujo unpubl. data. 2025). One reported Whale Shark from Sarawak, Malaysia, caught and locally consumed in 2018 further highlights that in densely-populated regions, small-scale fisheries might pose a higher threat to whale sharks than is currently understood (Araujo et al. 2022b, Reynolds et al. 2022).

Vessel strike
Vessel strikes have been a documented source of Whale Shark mortality for decades (i.e., Gudger 1941). Rapid increases in both the speed and quantity of marine traffic mean that mortality from ship strikes is suspected to have supplanted fisheries as the main contemporary threat to Whale Sharks in parts of their distribution (Rowat et al. 2021b). Global shipping maps show that vessel traffic is extensive across both coastal and oceanic waters, with Whale Sharks at risk of collision across the majority of their global range. Overall, 92% of mean monthly (satellite-tracked) Whale Shark activity overlapped with large >300 gross ton vessels in 2011–2014, and tracked sharks spent almost half of their time in surface waters <20 m deep, where they can be susceptible to collisions (Womersley et al. 2022). Whale Sharks in areas where there are large aggregations adjacent to heavy vessel traffic, such as the Gulf of Mexico and northern Caribbean Sea (de la Parra et al. 2011, Womersley et al. 2024a) and the Arabian/Persian Gulf (Robinson et al. 2013, Reynolds et al. 2022, Womersley et al. 2024a), are at particularly high risk, with the type of large vessels most likely to impact the species varying across aggregation sites (Womersley et al. 2024a). Direct records of mortality are rare, as the sharks typically sink if killed (Speed et al. 2008, Womersley et al. 2022), but probable deaths have been recorded from satellite-tagged sharks (Womersley et al. 2022, R. Graham unpubl. data 2025), and major vessel related injuries are frequently observed in live Whale Sharks (Womersley et al. 2024a). Documented injuries may only constitute a small fraction of the real collision mortality risk, as Whale Sharks are unlikely to survive propeller or impact wounds from large vessels. 

Unregulated tourism 
Poor Whale Shark tourism practices, particularly those resulting in small vessel strikes, have been reported as a threat to the species at many aggregation sites (Womersley et al. 2024a). Though generally non-lethal, increasing Whale Shark tourism with a lack of effective risk management has been associated with declining abundance (Harvey-Carroll et al. 2021), increased injury rates (Harvey-Carroll et al. 2021, Penketh et al. 2021), and behavioural changes (Quiros 2007, Haskell et al. 2015, Thomson et al. 2017). Increases in the activity levels of Whale Sharks in association with tourism indicate an increase in their energetic costs (Barry et al. 2023, Reynolds et al. 2025). Careful regulation of tourism activities can reduce the real and potential threats associated with this sector (Rowat et al. 2021b, Ziegler and Dearden 2021). However, even “gold standard” (Ziegler and Dearden 2021) Whale Shark tourism at Ningaloo Reef has some impacts on Whale Shark activity levels and behaviour (Reynolds et al. 2025), and there is the potential for tourism to induce as-yet unknown physiological effects on the species. As tourism activities tend to occur in specific aggregation areas, usually dominated by juvenile male sharks, and close to the necessary infrastructure, tourism likely affects a minority of the global Whale Shark population and results in minimal mortality. 

Pollution
The Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010 in the northern Gulf of Mexico affected a known Whale Shark habitat (Campagna et al. 2011, Frias-Torres and Bostater 2011), potentially causing mortalities or changes in movement behaviour (Hueter et al. 2013). Although there is extensive oil and gas production close to significant Whale Shark aggregation areas, such as the Gulf of Mexico (Hoffmayer et al. 2005, Hueter et al. 2013, McKinney et al. 2017, Hoffmayer et al. 2021), the Arabian/Persian Gulf (Robinson et al. 2013, 2016, 2017), and Ningaloo Reef in Australia (B. Norman pers. obs.), the regionally restricted nature of the industry means that localised spills are likely to affect a minority of the global Whale Shark population.
'Red tides,' caused by toxic blooms of Karenia spp. dinoflagellates, are associated with nutrient run-off and are increasing in frequency along the southern US coast (Brand and Compton 2007). These often result in shark mortality (Flewelling et al. 2010), among many other marine species, and the first probable Whale Shark mortality from this cause was reported in Florida in 2018 (Furby 2018). 

Plastic pollution can affect filter-feeding sharks and rays (Germanov et al. 2018). Whale Sharks can accidentally ingest large quantities of microplastics while feeding in some areas, with up to about 137 pieces per hour reported from Java in Indonesia (Germanov et al. 2019). Whale Shark mortalities from plastic ingestion have been reported from Japan (Matsumoto et al. 2017, Rowat et al. 2021a), Malaysia (Lee 2019, Rowat et al. 2021b), the Philippines (Abreo et al. 2019), and Thailand (Haetrakul et al. 2009). A variety of other sublethal effects are also possible, such as endocrine disruption or toxicosis (Germanov et al. 2018). Investigation of anthropogenic pollutants, such as heavy metals, PCBs and DDT, in Whale Sharks is a recent area of study (Boldrocchi et al. 2020), with PCBs and DDT in shark skin tissue present in the Gulf of California (Fossi et al. 2017) and Djibouti (Boldrocchi et al. 2020). Entanglement, particularly in discarded or lost fishing gear, is also a likely source of mortality (Wilcox et al. 2016, Parton et al. 2019).

Climate change
Cyclical or longer-term climate shifts affect Whale Shark occurrence and local abundance (Sleeman et al. 2010, Sequeira et al. 2012), which needs to be considered when discussing local population trends. Further, a minor expansion of Whale Sharks' seasonal penetration into higher latitudes appears to be underway, in conjunction with increasing ocean temperatures (see Distribution section), and this poleward movement is projected to increase under current climate change scenarios (Sequeira et al. 2014, Reynolds et al. 2024, Womersley et al. 2024b). However, model predictions suggest that the overall range of the Whale Shark may slightly decrease over time, due to a decrease in habitat suitability in some areas of their existing distribution (Sequeira et al. 2014, Reynolds et al. 2024, Womersley et al. 2024b). Oceanographic factors other than temperature will also likely impact Whale Sharks in future climate scenarios. In particular, decreasing dissolved oxygen availability is increasingly raised as a key concern for pelagic sharks, given its potential to reduce overall habitat volume (Laffoley and Baxter 2019, Lawson et al. 2019, Waller et al. 2024). At this stage, while climate change may affect a majority of Whale Sharks, it appears that their broad thermal tolerance and wide distribution may buffer them from direct mortality. However, the potential for ecosystem-level effects on prey species, notably impacts to fish spawning aggregations that provide concentrated food sources (Graham and Roberts 2005), and cumulative exposure to other threats means that climate change remains a significant concern.
documentation.measures:
The Whale Shark has been listed in a number of international conventions and agreements, summarized by Pierce et al. (2021a). 

The species is included in Annex I (Highly Migratory Species) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which provides a framework for the conservation and management of fisheries, and other uses of the seas. To date, no management initiatives enacted through UNCLOS have included the Whale Shark.

The Whale Shark was listed on Appendix II of the Bonn Convention for the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) in 1999 and Appendix I in 2017. As of 2022, CMS had 133 Parties, with many Whale Shark range states included (Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals 2025). Parties to CMS should '... endeavour to strictly protect them by: prohibiting the taking of such species, with very restricted scope for exceptions; conserving and where appropriate restoring their habitats; preventing, removing or mitigating obstacles to their migration and controlling other factors that might endanger them' (Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals 2025). The Whale Shark is also listed on Annex I of the CMS Sharks Memorandum of Understanding, a non-legally binding instrument that aims to facilitate a favourable conservation status for migratory sharks. As of 2025, there were 49 signatories to the Sharks MOU, which aims to improve scientific knowledge, ensure fisheries sustainability, protect critical habitats, movement corridors, and life stages of sharks, while increasing public participation and national, regional and international cooperation towards these objectives.

The Whale Shark was listed on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES) in 2003. Exports from CITES Parties need to be accompanied by permits based on findings that parts are sourced from legal and sustainable fisheries. 

A number of range states have species-specific legal protections in place for Whale Sharks, and other countries have prohibited any commercial fishing of sharks in their exclusive economic zones (EEZ), creating a 'shark sanctuary' (Pierce et al. 2021a). With these included, national- or territory-level protection measures for Whale Sharks are known to be in place in American Samoa, Australia, Bahamas, Bangladesh, Belize, Brazil, British Virgin Islands, Cabo Verde, Cambodia, Caribbean Netherlands, Cayman Islands, Chagos Archipelago, China, Colombia, Congo-Brazzaville, Cook Islands, Costa Rica, Curacao, Djibouti, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, French Polynesia, Gabon, Grenada, Guatemala, Guadeloupe, Guyana, Honduras, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), Indonesia, India, Israel, Kuwait, Maldives, Malaysia, Marshall Islands, Mayotte (France), Mexico, Micronesia, Mozambique, Myanmar, New Caledonia, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Pakistan, Palau, Panama, Peru, Philippines, Reunion, Saudi Arabia, Seychelles, South Africa, St Helena Island (UK), St Maarten, Taiwan, Tanzania, Thailand, Tokelau, United Arab Emirates, United States of America, and Wallis and Futuna (France). However, species-level legislative protection remains an important conservation goal in some countries where significant Whale Shark aggregations are present, including Madagascar (Diamant et al. 2021), Oman, and Qatar (Robinson et al. 2016). Whale Sharks are also present, seasonally or year-round, in many marine protected areas throughout their distribution, including some that have been purposefully set up to protect important Whale Shark habitats, such as the Whale Shark Biosphere Reserve in Mexico.

As the two major ongoing threats to the global Whale Shark population, fishing (particularly large-scale net fisheries) and vessel strike are the highest priorities for conservation intervention. Targeted catches of Whale Sharks are now likely to be rare, and can be reduced further by continued efforts to end illegal trade. Further data on incidental catch in nets, including the number of Whale Sharks entangled and their locations, will allow for conservation actions to reduce this source of mortality. Training in safe release practices for Whale Sharks caught in net fisheries, as has been implemented in India (Akhilesh et al. 2013) and Pakistan (Razzaque et al. 2020), is an important facet of this work.

Vessel strike mitigation measures have successfully been implemented for large cetacean species (Schoeman et al. 2020). The small spatial extent and known seasonality of many Whale Shark aggregations mean that targeted re-routing of shipping routes or speed reductions are likely to be similarly effective in reducing Whale Shark injury and mortalities (Womersley et al. 2024a).
documentation.use_trade:
Historically, Whale Sharks have been subject to target fisheries driven by, in some areas, local consumption and use, and the international trade of derivative products. Animals incidentally caught are often utilized, and some national and international trade occurs. Whale Sharks are also a focal species for wildlife tourism industries in many countries.

Atlantic Ocean
Occasional Whale Shark catches have occurred in the Atlantic Ocean since at least 1912 (Gudger 1941). A targeted fishery was present in Santa Cruz, Cuba, where 8–9 sharks were caught each year until the fishery was banned in 1991 (Graham 2007). In Venezuela, two Whale Sharks were reportedly harpooned by fishers prior to 1976 (Romero et al. 2000), and up to 21 sharks were opportunistically caught between 2014–2017 and their fins sold (Sánchez et al. 2020). Following targeted conservation efforts between 2018–2020, no further retention was reported from this fishery (Sánchez et al. 2020). There are no other records of targeted catches of Whale Sharks or trade from this subpopulation.

Indo-Pacific
Extensive use and trade have occurred in the Indo-Pacific region. Here, Whale Sharks have been caught commercially in fisheries since at least the 1850s (Gudger 1941), including for the international export of their fins (e.g., from India to China; Bean 1907). However, before the 1980s, they were rarely targeted (Silas 1986, Hsu et al. 2012, Acebes 2013), but rather harpooned opportunistically or landed as incidental catch. Whale Shark muscle tissue has a high water content and has generally been considered unpalatable, or at least of low value, across much of their distribution (Silas 1986, Colman 1997, Acebes 2013). The liver was the primary reason for catches being landed in many areas, as the liver oil could be used as a preservative for the timber used in boat hulls (Silas 1986, Anderson and Ahmed 1993, Hanfee 2001, Akhilesh et al. 2013). Some Whale Sharks were taken specifically for their liver in India as early as 1955–1960 (Hanfee 2001). Fishers in the Maldives used to take 20–30 individuals per year for their oil, but reported declining catches during the 1980s to early 1990s (Anderson and Ahmed 1993), and the fishery was banned in 1995. Occasional hunting may have continued following protection (Riley et al. 2009). 

Prior to 1985, there was little demand for Whale Shark meat in Taiwan, although the species was caught regularly as incidental catch in set-net fisheries (Chen et al. 1997). Specimens of several tons in weight sold at US$200–300 (Chen and Phipps 2002). A meat fishery developed during the 1990s, with annual catches accelerating to 272 individuals in 1996, derived from both set-net and harpoon fisheries. Whale Shark became the most expensive shark meat available in Taiwan by 1997, reaching prices of US$13.93/kg. A small 2 tonne (t) Whale Shark could by then fetch US$14,000, with a larger 10 t shark selling for around US$70,000 in 1997 (Chen et al. 1997). Catches declined from this peak to 80–100 sharks throughout the country each year after 1997 (Hsu et al. 2012). The annual volume of Whale Shark meat traded more than doubled between 1998 and 2000, however, to 60 t in 2000 (Chen and Phipps 2002). Market surveys in 2001 indicated that catches were being under-reported in official statistics and that significant quantities of Whale Shark meat were also being imported through unofficial channels (Chen and Phipps 2002). Following the introduction of specific export codes for Whale Shark meat in 2001, no imports and 2 t of exports were recorded over the following year—mostly to Spain, and valued at US$1.15/kg (Chen and Phipps 2002). Concern for the status of the species led to total allowable catch quotas being steadily reduced down to zero sharks over the 2001–2007 period (Hsu et al. 2012). A total of 693 sharks were caught in Taiwan between 2001 and 2008 (Hsu et al. 2012). Whale Sharks are still regularly encountered in Taiwan’s set net fisheries but, since 2007, they have been released by fishers once caught due to comprehensive fishing bans (Hsu et al. 2012). 

The increase in value and demand for Whale Shark meat in Taiwan led to buyers seeking international suppliers (Hanfee 2001, Chen and Phipps 2002, Acebes 2013). In the Bohol Sea of the Philippines, this led to former marine mammal hunters switching to Whale Sharks, and the improved profit enabled boat owners to invest in larger, faster vessels (Acebes 2013). From 1990 to 1997, 624–627 Whale Sharks were caught from four of the primary fishing sites in the Philippines (Alava and Dolumbaló 2002). When Whale Sharks were protected in the Maldives and the Philippines in 1998, Indian exporters realised that Whale Shark exports could prove lucrative and encouraged more fishers there to start targeting the species (Hanfee 2001). Between 1889 and 1998, 1,974 Whale Sharks were recorded as landed in India (Pravin 2000). Surveys in Gujarat from 1999 to 2000 recorded about 600 Whale Sharks landed, with some additional reports received following the cessation of on-site catch monitoring (Hanfee 2001). Following a conservation campaign, Whale Sharks were legally protected in Indian territorial waters in 2001 (Akhilesh et al. 2013). However, landings of Whale Sharks are still documented across India, especially on the coast Andhra Pradesh (e.g., Sathiyaselvam et al. 2016), and in many cases derivative products such as meat are utilised by coastal communities. Similarly, in Pakistan, commercial fisheries for Whale Shark were closed in the 1970s. However, if landed, animals are consumed locally or used as raw material for fishmeal, while fins enter the international trade (Moazzam Khan pers. comm. 03/06/2025).

Whale Shark meat from mainland China was historically likely also exported to the Taiwanese market (Chen and Phipps 2002). Though Whale Sharks were not necessarily targeted off mainland China, there was a large incidental catch, estimated at more than 1,000 individuals per annum, due to the intense fishing pressure of the Chinese fleet (Li et al. 2012). Whale Sharks were considered to be a high-value catch in the fishery (Li et al. 2012). An NGO exposé on the "planet's biggest slaughter of Whale Sharks" at Puqi markets in Zhejiang province, reported that at least 600 Whale Sharks were processed per year based on investigations from 2010 to 2013 (WildLifeRisk 2014). After the meat, the most profitable product was liver oil, which was extracted for use in cosmetics and health supplements (WildLifeRisk 2014). Whale Shark filter pads also have commercial value in Chinese trade, likely as a substitution for mobulid ray gill plates (O'Malley et al. 2017, Steinke et al. 2017). Reports from Puqi, which remains the most important processing hub for sharks in China, suggest that the scale of the shark fishing industry overall has substantially contracted in recent years (Wu 2016). This may indicate a decline in the number of Whale Sharks being caught, although small quantities of Whale Shark products have been reported from Chinese trade surveys (O'Malley et al. 2017, Steinke et al. 2017). The current status of the Chinese Whale Shark fishery is unclear.

Whale Shark fins can also have high trade value (McClenachan et al. 2016). While international trade in Whale Shark fins has taken place for well over a century (Bean 1907), they were regarded as low value in Taiwan in the 1990s due to poor quality and the difficulty of their preparation (Chen and Phipps 2002). Demand for Whale Shark fins within the broader shark fin trade was minimal, despite sometimes being sold as display fins for shark fin soup restaurants (Chen and Phipps 2002). A survey of the Indian fishery, however, found that the fins were a high-value export product to Hong Kong SAR, Singapore, Taiwan, and the USA; fishers were paid up to US$1,100 per set of fins in 1999 (Hanfee 2001). Chinese surveys found that Whale Shark fins obtained high prices (Li et al. 2012, WildLifeRisk 2014). Occasional reports of Whale Shark fins and meat being taken in various countries, including Bangladesh (Haque et al. 2019), off Ecuador (Bonaccorso et al. 2021), the Maldives (Riley et al. 2009), Indonesia (White and Cavanagh 2007), and Venezuela (Sánchez et al. 2020), and their occasional presence in trade surveys (O'Malley et al. 2017, Steinke et al. 2017), indicate that some international trade may persist, though domestic use for catches cannot be ruled out in some of these cases.

After starting at Ningaloo Reef in Western Australia in the 1980s, tourism industries based on swimming with or viewing Whale Sharks have now developed at 27 wild sites in 19 countries or territories, as well as eight sites where Whale Sharks are provisioned, and multiple aquarium exhibits (Ziegler and Dearden 2021). For example, in the Philippines, there are at least three provisioning sites in southern Bohol developed in 2019–2024, hosting 1–15 individuals daily, and in northern Mindanao Whale Sharks are seasonally encountered (November–May) in Macajalar, Gingoog and Butuan bays (Alava and Dolumbaló 2002, Eckert et al. 2002, Araujo et al. 2018). Excluding aquaria, sites around the world attract around 980,000 people, with an economic value of more than US$139 million in 2019 (Ziegler and Dearden 2021).
documentation.rationale: The Whale Shark (Rhincodon typus) is a large (to 18–20 m total length) shark that occurs across tropical and warm temperate oceans. This highly mobile species is found in coastal and oceanic habitats to a depth of at least 1,928 m. Genetic results indicate that two major subpopulations exist, in the Atlantic Ocean and Indo-Pacific, respectively. Pronounced size- and sex-based segregation is present in most of the species’ known feeding and transit areas, with coastal sites typically dominated by juvenile male sharks. The largest known aggregation sites for Whale Sharks host hundreds or low thousands of individuals, based on identified individual sharks and model estimates. Although individual sharks are highly mobile, many show a degree of site fidelity, and limited direct connectivity has been observed across large geographical scales. Major contemporary threats at the global level include incidental catch in a wide range of net fisheries and serious injury and inferred mortality through vessel strikes. If landed, the meat is consumed locally and the fins are likely to enter international trade. Target and incidental catch fisheries have impacted Whale Sharks in the Indo-Pacific, and there is substantial evidence for a reduction of large adult sharks, decreases in catch-per-unit-effort from fisheries, and declining sightings-per-unit-effort from fisheries and sight-resight studies. While a number of commercial fisheries for the species closed during the 1990–2000s, the species still faces a significant level of threat. Based on count data, modelled population estimates and habitat availability, 75% of the global Whale Shark population is inferred to occur in the Indo-Pacific, and 25% in the Atlantic. An overall decline of >65% is inferred in the Indo-Pacific over the last 120 years (three generations), resulting in a subpopulation assessment of Endangered. In the Atlantic Ocean, the overall population decline is considered to be lower at ≥30%, resulting in a subpopulation assessment of Vulnerable. Given the bulk of the global population occurs in the Indo-Pacific, based on abundance data and actual levels of exploitation, a population reduction of 50–79% was inferred over the last three generations (120 years). Therefore, the species is assessed as Endangered A2bd.
